caves.title: How Caves Form
caves.text:
Caves are not carved out in a single dramatic event. Most of the world's caves develop gradually, as ordinary water dissolves solid rock across spans of time that are difficult to imagine.

The process originates above ground. Rainwater seeps through soil, and as it does, it absorbs carbon dioxide, which dissolves into the water and converts it into a weak carbonic acid. This acid is far too mild to injure a person, yet across thousands of years its effect becomes considerable.

The acidified water continues descending until it reaches a layer of limestone. That rock matters here because it dissolves readily in acid, while many surrounding rock types do not. The water does not attack the limestone evenly; instead, it enters through fractures, joints, and other weaknesses already present in the stone.

Once inside, the acid dissolves the surrounding rock, and every fracture becomes slightly wider. That widening is important, because a larger opening permits greater water flow, and additional water delivers additional acid. The process therefore accelerates itself, and a passage opens faster as it develops.

Even so, the overall rate remains remarkably slow. A passage containing an active stream may widen by about one millimeter each year. At that rate, a tunnel large enough to walk through represents many thousands of years of dissolving, and extensive cave systems are often hundreds of thousands of years old.

key_points.point: Water picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit any mention that the water becomes acidic. Mentioning carbon dioxide alone also counts.

key_points.point: The acidic water reaches limestone, which dissolves in acid while many other rocks do not.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit naming limestone, or describing a rock that dissolves while others do not.

key_points.point: The water gets in through cracks, joints, and weak spots already in the rock.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit cracks, gaps, holes, splits, or weak spots that already existed.

key_points.point: As rock dissolves the openings widen, letting more water and acid through, so the process speeds itself up.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit any description of openings getting bigger AND that letting more water in. Credit 'it speeds up' or 'feeds itself'.

key_points.point: The process is extremely slow, roughly a millimeter a year, so caves take many thousands of years.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit any mention of the process being very slow or taking thousands/millions of years.

quiz.q: What makes the water able to dissolve the rock?
options: It is heated deep underground
It picks up carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic
It carries sand that scrapes the rock away
It freezes and cracks the rock apart

quiz.q: Why does limestone matter in cave formation?
options: It is softer than the soil above it
It holds heat from deep in the earth
It dissolves in acid, while many other rocks do not
It stops water from sinking any further

quiz.q: Where does the water first get into the rock?
options: Through cracks and weak spots already in the stone
Through holes dug by animals
Evenly across the whole rock surface
Through the tops of underground streams

quiz.q: Why does the process speed up over time?
options: The acid grows stronger as it ages
The rock becomes softer as it gets older
Underground streams heat the water
Wider openings let more water and more acid through

quiz.q: About how fast does a passage with a stream in it widen?
options: About a meter per year
About a centimeter per year
About a millimeter per year
About a kilometer per century

geysers.title: How Geysers Work
geysers.text:
Geysers do not erupt unpredictably. A geyser is essentially a hot spring with an unusual underground geometry, and that geometry is what causes it to erupt violently rather than steaming quietly.

The crucial difference is a narrow section. Somewhere within a geyser's underground plumbing, typically near the surface, the channel contracts into a constriction. In an ordinary hot spring, water circulates freely and heat escapes at the surface. The constriction blocks that circulation, so heat accumulates instead of escaping.

Confined beneath the narrowed section, the water grows steadily hotter. Normally it would simply boil, but the water above it is substantial, and its weight exerts downward pressure. That additional pressure raises the temperature at which water boils, so water deep in the system can exceed its ordinary boiling point while remaining liquid.

Such a balance cannot last forever, and as water gradually rises, steam bubbles begin forming. These bubbles expand as they rise, and near the surface they displace the water above them through the vent, causing the geyser to splash and overflow.

That overflow is what triggers the eruption. Losing water from the top substantially reduces the pressure below, and the superheated water underneath flashes violently into steam. The expanding steam propels a column of water out of the ground, and the eruption continues until the water drains faster than it can be refilled.

key_points.point: A geyser is a hot spring whose underground channel has a narrow constriction.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit any mention of a narrow/tight/pinched spot in the underground channel or plumbing.

key_points.point: The constriction stops the water from circulating, so heat builds up instead of escaping.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit heat being trapped, building up, or not escaping, or water not being able to circulate.

key_points.point: The weight of the water above adds pressure, raising the boiling point so the water superheats without boiling.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit pressure or the weight of water keeping it from boiling, or water getting hotter than its normal boiling point.

key_points.point: Steam bubbles form and rise, pushing water out the top so the geyser overflows.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit bubbles or steam rising and pushing water out, or the geyser spilling/overflowing first.

key_points.point: The overflow drops the pressure, the superheated water flashes into steam, and that drives the eruption until the water runs out or cools.
key_points.scoring_note: Credit the pressure drop causing the eruption, or the eruption ending when water runs out or cools.

quiz.q: What makes a geyser different from an ordinary hot spring?
options: It sits directly on top of a volcano
Its underground channel has a narrow constriction
Its water comes from rain rather than from underground
It contains far more dissolved minerals
It filters sand out of the water
It cools the water before it reaches the surface
It stops the water from circulating, so heat builds up
It lets steam escape slowly and steadily

quiz.q: Why can the water get hotter than its normal boiling point without boiling?
options: The water is unusually pure
A layer of steam insulates it from above
The surrounding rock absorbs most of the heat
The weight of the water above adds pressure, raising the boiling point

quiz.q: What happens just before the eruption?
options: Steam bubbles rise and push water out, making the geyser overflow
The water near the surface freezes
The constriction widens
Cold water floods in from the surface

quiz.q: What brings an eruption to an end?
options: The constriction closes up
The water drains faster than it refills, or the system cools
The steam turns back into liquid water
Rain cools the surface of the pool
